lesson.title: Drawing the Line: George Kennan and the Strategy of Containment
lesson.summary: American diplomat George Kennan argued that the Soviet Union could not be reformed or appeased, only patiently contained, and his idea became the guiding strategy of American foreign policy for the next four decades.
lesson.body:
As tensions with the Soviet Union deepened in 1946 and 1947, American officials needed more than a description of the problem; they needed a strategy. That strategy came from George Kennan, the same diplomat whose Long Telegram had warned Washington about Soviet intentions. In July 1947 Kennan published an article in the journal Foreign Affairs, signed only "X" to preserve his anonymity as a government official, titled "The Sources of Soviet Conduct." In it he argued that the Soviet Union, driven by both communist ideology and a long tradition of Russian insecurity, would probe for weaknesses and expand wherever it met no resistance.

Kennan's proposed answer was containment: the United States should not try to invade or overthrow the Soviet Union, nor should it try to appease Soviet demands the way Britain and France had appeased Hitler in the 1930s. Instead, Kennan wrote that the United States needed "a long-term, patient but firm and vigilant containment of Russian expansive tendencies," applying counterpressure at a series of shifting geographical and political points wherever the Soviets threatened to expand. The goal was not a quick victory but a long standoff, one Kennan believed the Soviet system would eventually lose because of its own internal weaknesses.

Containment became the intellectual foundation for nearly every major American foreign policy decision of the Cold War that followed, from economic aid programs to military alliances to wars fought on the other side of the world. It offered a middle path between two extremes many Americans feared, all out war with the Soviet Union on one hand and a retreat into isolationism on the other. Over time American leaders applied Kennan's idea more broadly and more militarily than he originally intended, something Kennan himself later criticized, but the basic logic, that communist expansion anywhere had to be met with resistance, shaped American policy from the late 1940s all the way to the collapse of the Soviet Union decades later.
